meta.description: Stax supplement dataset. Thirteen supplements. Every form rating and every rule points to entries in `sources`.

absorption.higher: Absorbed better than the reference form of this supplement
absorption.similar: No meaningful difference from the reference form
absorption.lower: Absorbed worse than the reference form
absorption.unclear: Claims exist but the data are too thin or conflicting to rate

evidence.strong: Multiple controlled human studies or a meta-analysis agree
evidence.moderate: At least one decent controlled human study, not yet well replicated
evidence.weak: Small, indirect, or differently-measured studies only
evidence.marketing: Claim circulates commercially with no supporting human data

ruleType.avoid: Do not place in the same slot; respect gapHours if given
ruleType.pair: Bonus for placing in the same slot
ruleType.doseWarning: Not a timing rule. Show a warning when the combined daily dose crosses a threshold
ruleType.medication: Flag-only. Never scheduled; shown as a warning with the timing gap
ruleType.dailyNote: Not a timing rule. An effect on the day's total balance; shown as info, never moves a supplement
ruleType.preferApart: Soft separation: a different time is preferred when it costs little, but the pair may share a time. Used where human evidence conflicts.
ruleType.noInteraction: Checked and not supported: no effect on scheduling. When both items share a time, the plan explains why that's fine, with sources.

gapBasis.measured: The gap was tested directly in a study
gapBasis.convention: The interaction is sourced, but the specific gap length is a common clinical convention, not a measured value

withFood.preferred: Meal slots score higher; waking slot allowed

limitKind.UL: Tolerable upper intake level: the highest daily intake considered unlikely to cause harm
limitKind.safe-level: No firm upper limit could be set; this is the highest intake the authority judged safe
limitKind.guidance: Not a formal upper limit; an authority's statement that intakes up to this amount are safe
limitKind.none: No upper limit has been set, usually because of low toxicity or too little data

solverNotes: avoid rules are symmetric: a rule on A against B also blocks B against A. Each pair is stored once.
Rules whose `with` target is not in the user's stack are ignored.
Targets listed in `externalRefs` are not yet full dataset entries; they exist so rules can reference them now.
Contexts are fixed anchors from user settings (times of day). A supplement rule pointing at a context blocks a window around each occurrence instead of a slot.

researchedNoRule.topic: Coffee or tea and zinc absorption
researchedNoRule.finding: No human absorption study found. Claims online trace back to rat studies or unsourced figures. No rule added.
Antithiamine claims exist, but the human studies could not be retrieved for verification. No rule added yet.
Only cell-culture data found. No rule added.

researchedNoRule.topic: Calcium and magnesium competing for absorption
researchedNoRule.finding: Not supported by human studies at normal or supplemental doses. Stored as a noInteraction rule on magnesium so the plan can explain it.

Often claimed that vitamin C taken with selenite blocks its absorption. The one human isotope study verified found the opposite direction at the diet level: low vitamin C intake (about 20 mg/day) was linked to lower selenite absorption than 1 g/day. No timing rule added.

timingDefaults.defaultAvoidGapNote: Applied to avoid rules that give no gap of their own. Slots can be minutes apart (waking vs breakfast), so 'different slot' alone is not separation.

emptyStomach.note: A non-meal slot only counts as empty-stomach if it is at least 2 h after the previous meal and 1 h before the next. Common clinical convention, not a measured value.

meta.formTimingNote: A form may carry `timingOverride`, whose fields replace the supplement's timing fields for that form (e.g. calcium carbonate requires food, citrate does not).
meta.maxPerDoseNote: `timing.maxPerDose` splits a dose above the threshold across separate times. Only applied when the user entered a dose.

formListing.rule: Only forms with `listed: true` appear in the dropdown. Unlisted forms stay in the data so the reference form and rules remain intact.

extraOptions.not-sure: Uses the reference form for timing and rating; shows a note that checking the label gives a more accurate plan. 'Other / not listed' maps here too.
extraOptions.blend: Uses the strictest timing among the supplement's listed forms and rates absorption as unclear.

regions.note: The region toggle only changes which reference values are shown and which limits trigger warnings. Timing rules are the same in both.

meta.componentsNote: A combination product (doseMode 'components') has no single dose. Its `components` carry their own reference values; only components with an upper limit get a dose field. A component form may change limits (`reference`) or timing (`timingOverride`).
meta.claimsNote: euClaims are quoted word for word from the EU list of permitted health claims (Reg. 432/2012). A claim is only allowed on a product that contains enough of the nutrient: at least a 'source of' it (15% of the NRV per daily portion for supplements) unless conditions say otherwise. roleInBody is a plain-language summary of the NIH fact sheet; it is not a health claim.

slots.note: Slots are generated by the scheduler from the user's meal, wake, bedtime and drink times. Only slots that end up used are shown.

warfarin-vka.label: Warfarin and other vitamin K antagonists

acid-suppressants.label: Acid-reducing medicines (PPIs such as omeprazole, H2 blockers)

supplements.name: Vitamin D

forms.name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
forms.note: Reference form. Raises blood 25(OH)D more effectively than D2.

forms.name: Vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol)
forms.note: Less effective at raising 25(OH)D. The 2012 meta-analysis found the gap clearest with large bolus doses and not significant with daily dosing. A later, larger RCT using a daily 15 µg dose found D3 more than twice as effective. Both forms do raise vitamin D status.

timing.withFoodWhy: Fat-soluble, so it is absorbed with dietary fat. In one study peak plasma D3 was about 32% higher with a fat-containing meal than a fat-free one. A second study found no difference in 25(OH)D after 90 days between meal conditions, so the long-term benefit of timing is unproven.

mealAdvice.text: Make this a meal with some fat in it (eggs, oily fish, nuts, cheese, olive oil). It doesn't need to be a high-fat meal: in one study a low-fat meal absorbed vitamin D slightly better than a high-fat one, and both beat a fat-free meal.

notes: D and K are often sold together. Both are fat-soluble, so the solver will tend to place them in the same meal slot anyway. There is no sourced rule that taking them together improves absorption of either, so no pair rule is stored.

upperLimit.note: 1 µg = 40 IU, so 100 µg = 4,000 IU.
1 µg = 40 IU, so 100 µg = 4,000 IU.

roleInBody.text: Helps the gut absorb calcium and phosphorus, which are needed to build and keep bones. Also involved in muscle and nerve function and the immune system.

claims.text: Vitamin D contributes to normal absorption/utilisation of calcium and phosphorus
Vitamin D contributes to normal blood calcium levels
Vitamin D contributes to the maintenance of normal bones
Vitamin D contributes to the maintenance of normal muscle function
Vitamin D contributes to the maintenance of normal teeth
Vitamin D contributes to the normal function of the immune system
Vitamin D has a role in the process of cell division

forms.name: Vitamin K1 (phylloquinone)
forms.note: Reference form. Absorbed well from supplements but cleared from the blood within hours.

forms.name: Vitamin K2 as MK-7
forms.note: Absorbed at least as well as K1 and has a much longer half-life (about 3 days), so it builds up to stable blood levels with daily intake. Exact timing matters little.

forms.name: Vitamin K2 as MK-4
forms.note: At nutritional doses (60 to 420 µg), MK-4 was not detectable in serum, while MK-7 was. Small study (10 women). High-dose pharmaceutical MK-4 is a different situation and is not rated here.

timing.withFoodWhy: Fat-soluble. Absorbed in the small intestine via bile-dependent micelles, like dietary fat.
timing.slotFlexibilityWhy: MK-7's long half-life means time of day has little effect on blood levels.

mealAdvice.text: Make this a meal with some fat in it, since vitamin K is absorbed together with dietary fat.

rules.why: Vitamin K directly counteracts warfarin-type anticoagulants. People on these drugs need a consistent vitamin K intake. MK-7 doses of 50 µg/day or more may interfere with anticoagulant treatment in a clinically relevant way.
rules.action: Do not start, stop or change vitamin K without the prescriber's input.

upperLimit.note: No upper limit set (insufficient data).
No upper limit set because of low potential for toxicity.

roleInBody.text: Needed to activate proteins for blood clotting, made in the liver. Also activates proteins involved in bone metabolism.

claims.text: Vitamin K contributes to normal blood clotting

supplements.name: Magnesium

forms.name: Magnesium citrate
forms.note: Reference form. Dissolves well even without stomach acid and is consistently better absorbed than oxide. Has a laxative effect at higher doses.

forms.name: Magnesium chloride / lactate / aspartate
forms.note: Soluble salts with absorption similar to each other and clearly better than oxide.

forms.name: Magnesium glycinate (bisglycinate)
forms.note: Widely marketed as the best-absorbed form, but head-to-head data do not show it beating citrate. In a 2003 RCT an amino-acid chelate did not outperform citrate. In a 2024 crossover study bisglycinate did not significantly raise plasma magnesium while citrate did. Often reported as gentler on the gut, but there is little controlled data on that.

forms.name: Magnesium oxide
forms.note: High magnesium content per tablet, but poorly absorbed: about 4% fractional absorption in one study, and no better than placebo over 60 days in another. The large number on the label overstates what you actually absorb.

timing.withFoodWhy: Mainly for tolerability. High supplemental doses commonly cause diarrhoea, nausea and cramping.

rules.why: Magnesium-rich supplements reduce absorption of oral bisphosphonates.

Calcium and magnesium are often said to compete for absorption, but the human studies found no effect. Adding 1,000 mg/day calcium did not change magnesium absorption (50% vs 55%) or balance in 26 girls. A stable-isotope study found the same at 1,800 vs 800 mg calcium. In the other direction, 826 mg/day magnesium did not change calcium absorption in adult men.
rules.evidenceNote: The studies are small and mostly in adolescents. An Australian reference review notes one exception: very high calcium (about 2,600 mg/day) combined with high sodium increased magnesium loss.

notes: Very high zinc doses (142 mg/day) interfere with magnesium absorption. This is stored as a dose warning on zinc, not as a timing rule.

upperLimit.note: Applies to magnesium salts in supplements, water and fortified foods, not magnesium naturally in food.
Applies to magnesium from supplements and medicines only, not food or water.

roleInBody.text: A cofactor for over 300 enzyme systems, including those for energy production, protein synthesis, muscle and nerve function, and blood sugar and blood pressure control. About half of the body's magnesium is in bone.

claims.text: Magnesium contributes to a reduction of tiredness and fatigue
Magnesium contributes to electrolyte balance
Magnesium contributes to normal energy-yielding metabolism
Magnesium contributes to normal functioning of the nervous system
Magnesium contributes to normal muscle function
Magnesium contributes to normal protein synthesis
Magnesium contributes to normal psychological function
Magnesium contributes to the maintenance of normal bones
Magnesium contributes to the maintenance of normal teeth
Magnesium has a role in the process of cell division

forms.name: Zinc gluconate
forms.note: Reference form. About 61% fractional absorption from a 10 mg dose without food.

forms.name: Zinc citrate
forms.note: Absorption essentially identical to gluconate (61.3% vs 60.9%) in a stable-isotope crossover study.

forms.name: Zinc picolinate
forms.note: The 'best absorbed' reputation comes mainly from one 1987 study of 15 people. It measured hair, urine and red-cell zinc after 4 weeks, not absorption directly. There is no modern isotope comparison with citrate or gluconate.

forms.name: Zinc oxide
forms.note: Insoluble in water. About 50% absorption versus 61% for citrate and gluconate, and some people absorbed little or none. Likely depends on stomach acid.

timing.withFoodWhy: Absorption data above were measured without food. Phytates in grains, legumes and nuts bind zinc and reduce its absorption, so if zinc is taken with a meal, a lower-phytate meal is better.

mealAdvice.text: If zinc is taken with this meal, lighter on whole grains, beans and nuts is better: their phytates bind zinc.

rules.why: Taking 25 mg or more of supplemental iron at the same time reduces zinc absorption and plasma zinc. Iron in fortified foods does not have this effect.

Evidence conflicts on whether calcium reduces zinc absorption. In one study 600 mg calcium carbonate taken with a meal halved zinc absorption from that meal, and adding about 8 mg zinc to the calcium supplement cancelled the effect. Another study gave 500 mg calcium carbonate with a meal and found no change in zinc retention.
rules.evidenceNote: Two small human studies with opposite results. Kept as a soft preference rather than a hard rule.

rules.why: Zinc doses of 50 mg/day or more over weeks inhibit copper absorption and can cause copper deficiency.
Very high zinc doses interfere with magnesium absorption and balance. Far above normal supplement doses.
Zinc and these antibiotics bind each other in the gut, reducing absorption of both.
rules.action: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before, or 4 to 6 hours after, zinc.

rules.why: Zinc reduces the absorption and action of penicillamine.

upperLimit.note: Applies to food plus supplements combined.
Applies to food plus supplements combined.

roleInBody.text: Needed for the activity of about 100 enzymes. Involved in immune function, protein and DNA synthesis, wound healing, cell division, and taste and smell.

supplements.name: Iron

forms.name: Ferrous sulfate
forms.tolerability: Roughly doubles the odds of GI side effects versus placebo (OR 2.32 across 20 RCTs).
forms.note: Reference form and the standard used in most trials. Cheap and effective, but GI side effects are the main reason people stop taking it.

forms.name: Ferrous bisglycinate
forms.tolerability: About 64% fewer reported GI adverse events than other iron forms in a meta-analysis (pregnant women).
forms.note: In a meta-analysis of 17 RCTs it raised hemoglobin more than other iron forms in pregnant women. No significant difference was seen in children. Evidence in non-pregnant adults is limited, so the 'higher' rating applies to the populations studied.

timing.withFoodWhy: Common meal components inhibit non-heme iron absorption. About 165 mg calcium in a meal (from milk or cheese) cut absorption by 50 to 60%. Coffee and tea taken with food also cut it substantially. If iron causes stomach upset, the fallback is a light, low-calcium meal without coffee or tea.
timing.preferredSlotsWhy: Morning single doses were used in the dosing studies. Splitting the dose twice daily raised hepcidin, the hormone that blocks iron absorption.

frequencyOptions.label: Every other day
frequencyOptions.why: Each iron dose raises hepcidin for about a day, which reduces absorption of the next dose. Alternate-day dosing gave higher fractional absorption in iron-depleted and anaemic women. At equal total doses over 3 months it did not give higher ferritin, but it caused fewer GI side effects and less iron deficiency at 6 months.

nearbyMealAdvice.text: Keep this meal low in dairy and other calcium-rich food. About 165 mg calcium, given as milk or cheese, cut iron absorption from a meal by 50 to 60%.

rules.why: Calcium inhibits both non-heme and heme iron absorption, in a dose-related way, when taken in the same meal. Calcium carbonate taken without food did not inhibit ferrous sulfate in one study, but calcium citrate and phosphate did, and all calcium forms inhibited iron when taken with food.
Coffee polyphenols bind non-heme iron in the gut so it cannot be absorbed. A cup with a meal cut iron absorption by 39%, and stronger coffee cut it more. Adding milk does not reduce the effect.
rules.gapNote: Before-gap is measured: coffee 1 h before a meal had no effect. After-gap of 2 h is a conservative choice, because coffee 1 h after still inhibited as much as with the meal, while for tea a 1 h gap reduced the inhibition.

rules.why: Tea polyphenols are stronger iron blockers than coffee: 64% reduction with a meal in one study and 79 to 94% in another. Adding milk does not reduce the effect.
rules.gapNote: Before-gap is measured: coffee 1 h before a meal had no effect. After-gap of 2 h is a conservative choice, because coffee 1 h after still inhibited as much as with the meal, while for tea a 1 h gap reduced the inhibition.

rules.why: Herbal teas and cocoa also inhibit iron, in proportion to their polyphenol content: peppermint 84%, cocoa 71%, chamomile 47%.
rules.gapNote: Same windows as coffee and tea; no herbal-specific timing study.

rules.why: Ascorbic acid enhances non-heme iron absorption, but only when present at the same time. A large vitamin C dose at breakfast did not affect iron absorbed at lunch or dinner. The effect measured across a whole diet is much smaller than in single-meal tests.

notes: Zinc and iron interaction is stored on zinc (symmetric avoid rule).
Medication interactions (e.g. levothyroxine, PPIs) not yet added; pending a primary source for each.

Decaf coffee is not exempt by assumption: the iron effect comes from polyphenols, not caffeine. No study in the dataset tested decaf directly, so the app should treat decaf as coffee until one is sourced.

upperLimit.note: EFSA could not identify a clear threshold for harm, so it set a safe level of intake instead of an upper limit.
Applies to food plus supplements combined.

roleInBody.text: Part of haemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues, and of myoglobin, which stores oxygen in muscle. Also needed for growth, brain development and making some hormones.

supplements.name: Calcium

forms.name: Calcium carbonate
forms.note: Reference form. 40% calcium by weight, so fewer or smaller tablets. Needs stomach acid to dissolve, so take it with a meal. More likely than citrate to cause gas, bloating and constipation.

timingOverride.withFoodWhy: Carbonate needs stomach acid to dissolve. Taking it with a meal keeps absorption up, especially for people with low stomach acid.

forms.name: Calcium citrate
forms.note: Only 21% calcium by weight, so larger or more tablets. Does not depend on stomach acid and can be taken without food. A meta-analysis found it absorbed about 22 to 27% better than carbonate, both fasting and with meals. A later crossover study found the two equivalent, so the size of the advantage is uncertain.

timingOverride.withFoodWhy: Works without food, but all calcium supplements are absorbed somewhat better with a meal.

timing.withFoodWhy: All calcium supplements are absorbed better when taken with food.

maxPerDose.why: Absorption is highest at 500 mg or less per dose: about 36% of a 300 mg dose versus 28% of a 1,000 mg dose.

rules.why: Calcium supplements reduce levothyroxine absorption; the levothyroxine label warning names calcium carbonate specifically.
rules.action: Keep levothyroxine at least 4 hours away from calcium.

rules.why: Calcium binds quinolone antibiotics in the gut.
rules.action: Take the antibiotic at least 2 hours before or 2 hours after calcium.

rules.why: Calcium reduces dolutegravir absorption.
rules.action: Take dolutegravir 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium.

notes: The calcium–iron separation is stored on iron (symmetric avoid rule).
Coffee's small effect on calcium balance is stored on the coffee context.

upperLimit.note: Applies to food plus supplements combined.
2,500 mg for ages 19–50 and 2,000 mg from age 51, food plus supplements combined.

roleInBody.text: The most abundant mineral in the body. About 99% is in bones and teeth, where it forms their structure. The rest is used for muscle contraction, blood vessel function, nerve signalling and hormone release.

supplements.name: Vitamin C

forms.name: Ascorbic acid
forms.note: Reference form. As bioavailable as the vitamin C in orange juice or broccoli. The cheapest form.

forms.name: Ester-C (calcium ascorbate with metabolites)
forms.note: Same plasma levels and urinary excretion as plain ascorbic acid in one comparison. Another study found higher levels in white blood cells after 24 hours. No clear advantage at a higher price.

forms.name: Ascorbic acid with bioflavonoids
forms.note: No difference from plain ascorbic acid in plasma levels or urinary excretion.

forms.name: Liposomal vitamin C
forms.note: Nine of ten small studies reported higher blood levels than plain vitamin C (1.2 to 5.4 times higher peak). The formulations, doses and methods differed widely, and almost none measured uptake into cells or any health effect.

timing.withFoodWhy: No sourced effect of food on vitamin C absorption.

maxPerDose.why: Absorption is about 70 to 90% at 30–180 mg/day and falls below 50% above 1 g. Splitting a large dose keeps each part on the efficient end of that curve. The 1,000 mg split point is a convention.

notes: The iron pairing is stored on iron.

upperLimit.note: No upper limit set (insufficient data). High doses can still cause diarrhoea, nausea and cramps.
Applies to food plus supplements combined. High doses can cause diarrhoea, nausea and cramps.

roleInBody.text: Needed to make collagen, L-carnitine and some neurotransmitters, and acts as an antioxidant. Improves absorption of non-haem iron from plant foods and supports immune function.

claims.text: Vitamin C contributes to maintain the normal function of the immune system during and after intense physical exercise

forms.name: Natural triglyceride fish oil
forms.note: Reference form, as it occurs in fish.

forms.name: Re-esterified triglyceride (rTG) concentrate
forms.note: About 124% of natural fish oil's bioavailability in a 2-week comparison.

forms.name: Ethyl ester (EE) concentrate
forms.note: About 73% of natural fish oil in the same comparison. Strongly meal-dependent: absorption roughly tripled with a high-fat meal compared with a low-fat one.

timingOverride.withFoodWhy: Ethyl esters need fat-digesting enzymes released by a fatty meal; absorption roughly tripled with 44 g versus 8 g of fat.

mealAdvice.text: Take ethyl-ester fish oil with your largest, fattiest meal of the day: its absorption depends far more on dietary fat than other forms.

forms.name: Krill oil (phospholipid)
forms.note: Some studies found higher bioavailability than fish oil, others did not.

forms.name: Algal oil (vegan DHA/EPA)
forms.note: Usually in triglyceride form. In a small study DHA from algal oil was as bioavailable as from cooked salmon.

timing.withFoodWhy: A fat, absorbed with the fat in a meal. Triglyceride EPA absorption rose from 69% to 90% with a high-fat meal.

mealAdvice.text: Make this a meal with some fat in it.

rules.why: Fish oil may prolong clotting time with warfarin, though most research finds 3–6 g/day does not significantly change anticoagulation.
rules.action: Mention it to the prescriber; INR may be checked periodically.

upperLimit.note: No formal upper limit. EFSA considers up to about 5 g/day EPA+DHA from supplements safe.
No formal upper limit. FDA considers supplements providing up to 5 g/day EPA+DHA safe.

roleInBody.text: EPA and DHA are built into cell membranes throughout the body; DHA is concentrated in the retina, brain and sperm. They are also used to make signalling molecules (eicosanoids) that act on the heart, blood vessels, lungs and immune system.

supplements.name: Selenium

forms.name: L-selenomethionine
forms.note: Reference form and the most common. The body uses it like the amino acid methionine and builds it into proteins throughout the body, so it raises blood selenium more than inorganic forms. That stored selenium is not necessarily more useful: the selenium-dependent antioxidant enzyme rose equally with selenate.

forms.name: Selenium yeast (selenium-enriched yeast)
forms.note: Mostly selenomethionine, so it behaves like the reference form.

forms.name: Sodium selenite
forms.note: Inorganic form. Absorption is high for all common forms, up to about 90%. It is not built into body proteins the way selenomethionine is, so blood selenium rises less for the same dose. No head-to-head enzyme comparison with selenomethionine was verified.

forms.name: Sodium selenate
forms.note: Raised blood selenium less than selenomethionine over 32 weeks, but raised the selenium-dependent enzyme just as much.

timing.withFoodWhy: No sourced effect of food on absorption. Absorption is high, up to about 90%, for all common supplement forms.

upperLimit.note: Set in 2023, lowered from 300 µg. Based on hair loss as the earliest sign of excess. Adults who take supplements or eat Brazil nuts regularly are the ones likely to exceed it.
Applies to food plus supplements combined. Early signs of excess are garlic breath and a metallic taste; hair loss and brittle nails are the most common.

roleInBody.text: The eight B vitamins work mainly as coenzymes: they help turn food into energy, make DNA and red blood cells, and keep the nervous system working. Each one has its own role, listed below.

supplements.name: Vitamin E

forms.name: Natural (d-alpha-tocopherol, RRR)
forms.note: Reference form. The liver selects this form and puts it back into the blood, so the body keeps it longer. Labels write it as d-alpha-tocopherol or d-alpha-tocopheryl acetate/succinate.

forms.name: Synthetic (dl-alpha-tocopherol, all-rac)
forms.note: A mix of eight mirror-image forms, of which the body retains mainly one. With natural and synthetic taken together, blood and tissues held about twice as much natural form. Officially 2 mg synthetic counts as 1 mg vitamin E. Labels write it as dl-alpha-tocopherol (the 'l' gives it away).

forms.name: Mixed tocopherols
forms.note: Contains gamma, delta and beta tocopherols besides alpha. Limits and daily values count only the alpha-tocopherol on the label, so enter that amount as the dose.

timing.withFoodWhy: Vitamin E needs fat to be absorbed. A 400 IU capsule taken with a fat-free breakfast was barely absorbed, and blood levels rose in only 2 of 5 people. Toast with butter (17.5 g fat) gave much higher absorption than low-fat cereal or water.

mealAdvice.text: Make this a meal with some fat in it. A vitamin E capsule with a fat-free meal is barely absorbed.

upperLimit.note: Applies to alpha-tocopherol from all sources, natural or synthetic. Based on reduced blood clotting and bleeding risk. Does not apply to people on anticoagulant or antiplatelet medicines, for whom it is too high.
Applies to supplements of either form: about 1,500 IU natural or 1,100 IU synthetic. High doses may raise bleeding risk, including bleeding in the brain.

rules.why: Vitamin E can increase the risk of bleeding with anticoagulants such as warfarin.
rules.action: Ask the prescriber before taking vitamin E.

rules.why: Vitamin E can increase the risk of bleeding with antiplatelet medicines.
rules.action: Ask the prescriber before taking vitamin E.

notes: Doses are in mg of alpha-tocopherol. IU converts differently by form: 1 IU natural = 0.67 mg, 1 IU synthetic = 0.45 mg.
A vitamin E–vitamin K interaction is often claimed for high doses; not verified, so no rule.

roleInBody.text: An antioxidant in cell membranes that stops chain reactions of free radicals in fats. Also involved in immune function and cell signalling.

claims.text: Vitamin E contributes to the protection of cells from oxidative stress

supplements.name: Coenzyme Q10

forms.name: Ubiquinone, softgel in oil
forms.note: Reference form. CoQ10 is a waxy crystal that the gut cannot absorb as crystals. Softgels dissolve it in oil first, so it can join the fat micelles of a meal.

forms.name: Ubiquinol, softgel
forms.note: The reduced form. The body converts ubiquinone and ubiquinol back and forth, in the gut wall and in the blood. Studies comparing the two disagree; how the product is made seems to matter more than which form it contains.

forms.name: Ubiquinone, tablet or powder capsule
forms.note: Products that do not disperse the crystals first were absorbed about 75% less in the reviewed studies. The review's authors include a CoQ10 manufacturer.

timing.withFoodWhy: CoQ10 is fat-soluble and is absorbed the same way as dietary fat, in micelles formed with bile. Bile is released when you eat, so a meal with some fat helps. Direct trials of fed versus fasting intake are few.

mealAdvice.text: Make this a meal with some fat in it.

upperLimit.note: No EU upper limit and no legal maximum for supplements. Germany allows up to 100 mg/day in supplements. Mild stomach upset was reported at up to 300 mg/day; higher doses have not been studied well.
Not an official limit. A risk assessment by supplement-industry authors found no harm at up to 1,200 mg/day in trials (observed safe level).

rules.why: CoQ10 may interact with warfarin. In Germany, people on anticoagulants are advised to get medical advice before taking more than 100 mg/day.
rules.action: Ask the prescriber before taking CoQ10.

rules.why: CoQ10 may interact with insulin.
rules.action: Ask the prescriber before taking CoQ10.

rules.why: CoQ10 may not be compatible with some types of cancer treatment.
rules.action: Ask the treating team before taking CoQ10.

notes: The body makes its own CoQ10; food provides about 3–6 mg/day. No deficiency needing treatment is known in healthy people.
Absorption per dose is limited, so in studies two smaller doses gave higher blood levels than one large dose. Stax does not split CoQ10 automatically.

roleInBody.text: Made by the body and present in most cells, with the highest levels in the heart, liver, kidneys and pancreas. In the mitochondria it carries electrons in the chain that produces cellular energy (ATP); its reduced form, ubiquinol, also acts as an antioxidant.

euClaims.none: No authorised claims. CoQ10 is not on the EU list of permitted health claims; EFSA assessed six proposed claims in 2010 (energy, blood pressure, antioxidant, cognition, cholesterol, endurance).

coffee.label: Coffee
coffee.activeComponent: Polyphenols (chlorogenic acids). Caffeine is a separate, smaller effect on calcium and magnesium excretion.

rules.why: Each 6 fl oz cup of caffeinated coffee was linked to a calcium balance about 4.6 mg/day more negative, because caffeine slightly lowers calcium absorption efficiency. About 40 mg extra calcium per cup offsets it. This is a whole-day effect, not a timing one, so it never moves a supplement.

Caffeine raises urinary excretion of calcium and magnesium for at least 3 hours after intake. The review found the effect does not fade with regular use. In younger adults with adequate calcium intake, increased absorption may compensate. Older women appear not to compensate as well.

tea.label: Black or green tea
tea.activeComponent: Polyphenols (tannins, catechins). Roughly twice the iron-blocking effect of coffee per cup.

herbal-tea.label: Herbal tea or cocoa
herbal-tea.activeComponent: Polyphenols. Peppermint is close to black tea; chamomile is about half as strong.
